summary.text: The laws of thermodynamics are a small set of rules linking temperature, energy, heat, work and entropy in systems at equilibrium.
Four laws are accepted: the zeroth defines temperature, the first conserves energy, the second says entropy never decreases, and the third ties entropy to absolute zero.
Together they rule out perpetual motion machines, which would either make work from no energy input or turn heat spontaneously into work.

items.prompt: A thermometer reads the same in a cup of coffee and in a bowl of soup. What can you conclude if the two are put in contact?

options.label: Heat will flow from the coffee to the soup
Heat will flow from the soup to the coffee
The soup will cool until it reaches freezing
They are in thermal equilibrium and stay as they are

items.explain: If two systems are each in thermal equilibrium with a third, here the thermometer, they are in thermal equilibrium with each other.

items.prompt: An inventor shows a wheel that keeps doing useful work forever with no fuel and no outside energy. Which idea rules this out?

options.label: Energy cannot be created, so work must use up energy
Heat cannot be measured without a thermometer
Temperature is always one-dimensional
Every substance has a single fixed melting point

items.explain: The first law says energy cannot be created or destroyed, so a machine making work from no energy input is impossible.

items.prompt: An ice cube is dropped into a warm drink. Could the drink spontaneously get warmer while the ice gets colder?

options.label: Yes, since energy is conserved either way
Yes, but only if the drink is stirred
No, since heat does not pass by itself from cold to warm
No, since ice cannot take in any energy

items.explain: Under the second law, heat does not spontaneously pass from a colder body to a warmer one.

items.prompt: A flawless crystal of a pure substance is cooled closer and closer to absolute zero. What happens to its entropy?

options.label: It grows larger and larger without limit
It settles toward a fixed value, typically close to zero
It swings up and down more wildly
It turns negative once the crystal is cold enough

items.explain: The third law says entropy approaches a constant value as temperature approaches absolute zero, and for a well-ordered crystal that value is typically close to zero.

items.prompt: Why was a law numbered zero added after the first three laws were already established?

options.label: To correct a mistake in the second law
To give a self-consistent definition of temperature
To replace the idea of heat engines
To explain why perpetual motion machines fail

items.explain: The zeroth law was added to allow a self-consistent definition of temperature, resting on thermal equilibrium.

items.prompt: A machine claims to draw heat from the surrounding air and turn it all into work, with energy fully accounted for. What does thermodynamics say?

options.label: It is allowed, because no energy is created
It is allowed, but only in cold surroundings
It is forbidden, because it breaks the first law
It is forbidden, because heat does not spontaneously become work

items.explain: This is a perpetual motion machine of the second kind, which spontaneously converts thermal energy into mechanical work and is prohibited by the second law even though energy is conserved.

paragraphs.heading: Rules for heat and energy
paragraphs.text: The laws of thermodynamics are a short list of scientific laws about heat and energy. They define quantities such as temperature, energy and entropy that describe a system once it has settled into equilibrium. They also set out how work and heat in a process relate to each other. Their reach goes beyond thermodynamics: they are basic laws of physics and apply across the other natural sciences.

paragraphs.heading: The zeroth law
paragraphs.text: The zeroth law defines thermal equilibrium. If two systems are each in equilibrium with a third, then they are in equilibrium with each other. This gives a basis for defining temperature. Though it is more basic than the others, it was given its label only after the first three laws had been established.

paragraphs.heading: The first and second laws
paragraphs.text: The first law is the conservation of energy adapted to thermodynamic processes. When energy flows into or out of a system, the system's internal energy changes to match, and in an isolated system the total stays fixed. The second law says that in a natural process the combined entropy of the systems involved never goes down. One everyday result is that heat does not flow by itself from a colder body to a warmer one.

paragraphs.heading: The third law
paragraphs.text: The third law looks at the coldest limit. As temperature nears absolute zero, a system's entropy settles toward a fixed value. For most systems that value is close to zero. The exception is glasses, which are solids without a crystal structure.

paragraphs.heading: No machines that run for free
paragraphs.text: These laws describe facts found by experiment that rule certain things out, such as perpetual motion. The first law forbids a machine that makes work without any energy going in. The second law forbids a machine that turns heat into mechanical work all by itself. Together they shut the door on both kinds of perpetual motion machine.

paragraphs.heading: How the laws took shape
paragraphs.text: The laws grew out of work done in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. In 1824 Sadi Carnot wrote down the earliest principle, which later became the second law, in Reflections on the Motive Power of Fire, his book. By 1860, through scientists such as Rudolf Clausius and William Thomson, the first and second laws were in place. Walther Nernst set out the third law between 1906 and 1912, and Ralph H. Fowler coined the name zeroth law in the 1930s.
